newsitem.title: INDIA: FOCUS - Market expectations of India monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Market expectations of India monetary policy.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Saturday unveils its monetary policy for the second half of 1996/97 (April-March).
Following are the major expectations of market participants, based on a snap poll of bankers and analysts on Friday.
** CUT IN CASH RESERVE RATIO

- Bankers expect a cut in cash reserve ratios (CRR) as this will boost liquidity and is expected to spark a fall in interest rates. Expectatations on the size of the cut vary from one percentage point to 1.5. The current CRR is 12 percent.

- However some analysts say that liquidity with banks is already good and there is no need to increase it further. Traditionally, the second half of the year sees a rise in inflation. A loosening of monetary strings now could stoke inflationary pressures, they say.
** REDUCTION IN DEPOSIT INTEREST RATE CAP

- Bankers and analysts say a cut in deposit rates is a precursor to any significant cut in their lending rates. At present the RBI has fixed a cap of 11 percent per annum for deposits with maturities above 30 days upto one year. Banks are free to determine rates for longer maturities.
** REMOVAL OF EXPORT REFINANCE LIMITS
- Some bankers expect the RBI to phase out the export refinance window as it has said in the past that any reduction in cash reserve requirements would have to be offset by a cut in refinance limits.
- But most bankers feel this may not happen as export performance has been poor during the current year and a phasing out of export refinance would make banks reluctant to lend to exporters.
** REDUCTION IN EXPORT REFINANCE RATE

- Bankers expect a cut in the refinance rate charged by the RBI on export refinance to 10 percent per annum from 11 percent. This will enable them to reduce their export lending rates to corporates to 12 percent from 13 percent, they say.
** REMOVAL OF PENAL INTEREST ON EXPORTERS

- The RBI allows banks to charge commercial rates of interest on export credit which is not repaid within 90 days. This was done in January when the rupee was under severe pressure with importers scrambling to cover their exposures while exporters were delaying remittances hoping to get better rupee realisations as the Indian currency fell. Exporters say since the rupee is stable now, the clause should be removed. .
** ALLOWING BANKS TO LEND FCNR (B) FUNDS

- Bankers say permission to lend FCNR (B) funds in dollars to Indian firms would allow them to pass on the exchange risk and the cost of swapping funds to their customers. Corporates, for their part will have access to foreign currency funds at lower rates than they would be able to get in international markets.
** REMOVAL OF RESERVE REQUIREMENTS ON INTER-BANK BORROWINGS
- Bankers say this will reduce their cost of interbank borrowings and be a major step in the development of a term money market and would enable them to take positions beyond the immediate fortnight.
** RELAXATIONS OF COMMERCIAL PAPER NORMS

- Bankers say a relaxation in commercial paper (CP) norms is a must if the CP market is to take off. Some bankers expect the RBI to restore the stand-by facility, linked to capital adequacy norms or prudential requirements.
** FURTHER SHIFT TOWARDS LOAN SYSTEM OF LENDING

- At present the cash credit component of the maximum permissible bank finance is 40 percent and the loan component, 60 percent. Some bankers expect the cash credit system to be reduced to 25 percent and the loan component to be increased to 75 percent.
** INCREASE IN THE INVESTMENT LIMITS OF BANKS

- At present banks are allowed to invest five percent of their incremental deposits every year in corporate shares and debentures. Bankers expect this to be increased as this might result in a greater flow of funds to depressed equity markets.
